name: Spanish Monarchy (Philip II)

territory.border: hb:1530:Spain + hb:1530:Habsburg Netherlands + hb:1530:Naples + hb:1530:Sicily + hb:1530:Sardinia + hb:1530:Milan

areaKm2.note: world_1530 polygons on the sphere: Spain 490,467 + Habsburg Netherlands 61,054 + Naples 68,817 + Sicily 24,017 + Sardinia 21,927 + Milan 26,972 = 693,254 km2. The Netherlands polygon covers all 17 provinces, half of which were in revolt; low subtracts the rebel north. Americas and Portugal excluded.

population.note: Crowns of Castile and Aragon ~8.1M (HYDE via OWID population.csv: Spain 6.5M in 1500, 8.5M in 1600, interpolated; https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true) + Kingdom of Naples ~3.0M, Sicily ~1.0M, Duchy of Milan ~1.1M, Sardinia ~0.25M + the Netherlands provinces under royal control in 1580 (~1.5M of ~3M). Portugal (conquered Aug 1580) and the American viceroyalties are excluded. Low drops half the Netherlands and uses lower Italian figures.

urbanization.note: OWID urban share (de Vries based): Spain 13.8% (1500), 17.1% (1600); Italy 18.4% (1600); Belgium ~29%. Bairoch 5,000+ convention runs a little higher; mid 16%.

activePersonnel.note: Salaried forces under arms in 1580: Army of Flanders ~30,000-45,000 after the 1577-79 withdrawal of the Spanish tercios (Dutch States Army article: Parma had 93 infantry companies in late 1579; Army of Flanders peaked at 86,000 paper in 1574 and 63,455 effectives in 1588), Alba's army for Portugal ~35,000-40,000, Italian garrisons of Milan, Naples and Sicily ~15,000-20,000, North African presidios and Spanish guards ~8,000, galley infantry and crews ~10,000-15,000. Parker (Military Revolution p. 24, quoted at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Revolution) gives ~200,000 paper for the Spanish Monarchy in the 1590s; effective is lower.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: Neapolitan and Sicilian militia (battaglione) and Castilian urban and seigneurial levies callable within a month; the general Castilian militia was only organised in 1590-98.

supportPersonnel.note: Galley sailors and gunners (~100 galleys x ~60-80 non-rowing seamen = 6,000-8,000), artillery trains and engineers (~2,000), Atlantic squadron crews (~3,000), administration and staffs. Galley oarsmen (convicts, slaves, buonavoglia, ~20,000) are not counted as military personnel.

mobilizationRatio.note: Parker: Philip IV claimed 300,000 regulars and 500,000 militia (paper) in 1625 for a monarchy of ~20M (Military Revolution article); real wartime peaks under Philip II ~200,000 incl. foreign mercenaries, i.e. ~3-5% of the subject population.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Tercios and regiments of Spanish, Italian, Walloon and German pike and shot (Army of Flanders infantry; Alba's Portuguese army ~20,000 Spanish/Italian/German foot; Italian garrisons). Reconstruction, grade C.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical) to 0.75 (among the era best). Evidence: arquebus and heavy musket (introduced by Alba 1567) with pike; best infantry kit of the 1580s

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: veteran Spanish tercios the best infantry of the era (Parker, Army of Flanders); Walloon and German regiments weaker

count.note: Lancers and men-at-arms of the Guardas de Castilla and Italian companies; the Army of Flanders discharged its heavy cavalry in 1572 (Army of Flanders article).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: lance and plate, being replaced by pistol-armed cuirassiers elsewhere

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: professional companies

count.note: Light horse, mounted arquebusiers and herreruelos; the Army of Flanders cavalry was mainly light cavalry until the 1630s (Army of Flanders article).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: era-typical light horse; chronic horse shortage in Flanders

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: professional but small arm

count.note: Educated guess: field pieces with the Army of Flanders and Alba's Portuguese campaign plus Italian trains; fortress guns excluded.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Spanish foundries at Malaga and Mechelen, standardised calibres under Philip II

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: contract gunners

count.note: War galleys in royal service (Spain, Naples, Sicily) plus Genoese galleys on asiento: at Lepanto 1571 the Spanish Empire sent 49 galleys and Genoa 27 (Lepanto article, Konstam/Parker); the total galley establishment reached ~146 in 1574 (Thompson, War and Government in Habsburg Spain) and was cut after the 1578-81 truce with the Ottomans. Atlantic galleons were few before the Portuguese fleet was taken over.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: Mediterranean galleys with bow batteries, the Lepanto-winning type

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: veteran galley squadrons of Naples and Sicily

count.note: Educated guess: galliots, fragatas, zabras and pataches in Mediterranean and Biscay service.

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.75 (trained staff system, proven commanders). Evidence: Alba (Portugal 1580) and Alessandro Farnese of Parma, the era's leading generals; Council of War administration; slow centralised decision making from Madrid

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.75. Evidence: tercio esprit de corps, but repeated mutinies over pay (sack of Antwerp 1576)

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75. Evidence: Lepanto (1571) and the conquest of Portugal; pay arrears after the 1575 bankruptcy

weapons.note: Anchor: 5 (1600: arquebus/musket, pike, field cannon). Evidence: Alba introduced the heavy musket in 1567; pike-and-shot tercios

armor.note: Anchor: 5 (half-armor, cuirass). Evidence: morion and corselet for pikemen

ships.note: Anchor: 5 (galleons, ships of the line) vs 4 (galleys). Evidence: Mediterranean galley fleet, first Atlantic galleons; 1580 is before the galleon squadrons of the 1588 Armada

fortification.note: Anchor: 5 (trace italienne). Evidence: bastioned fortifications in Italy and the Low Countries, but most of the Netherlands frontier still medieval

logistics.note: Anchor: 4.7 between river transport and magazines. Evidence: the Spanish Road and its etapas (Parker, Army of Flanders) were the first planned military supply corridor

communications.note: Anchor: 4.8 between relay horses and early postal. Evidence: Taxis imperial postal service Madrid-Brussels; dispatches ~2 weeks

isr.note: Anchor: ISR uses the same years as the anchor table (1600 -> 5, 1805 -> 6). Evidence: cavalry screens, spies and merchant reports only; no aerial or signal intelligence

air.note: No aircraft or military balloons before 1783/1794.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 (2011 int$): Spain 1580 = 1,446; Italy 1580 = 2,458 (MPD 2020, Malanima series, centre-north weighted); Belgium 1550/1600 = 2,410/2,533. Mid ~1,600 is the population-weighted mix with southern Italy discounted to ~1,600. Low = Spain alone.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess: military and naval spending took most of Castilian crown revenue of ~8-10M ducats; bankruptcies in 1557, 1560, 1575 show it exceeded sustainable levels. Peacetime low.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: Castilian textiles (Segovia, Toledo), Basque iron and Milanese and Flemish crafts; agrarian economy ~70% of output.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: Castile imported Sicilian and Baltic grain in bad years; Sicily and Apulia were grain exporters.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.009-0.011 (mid 0.0095): in a pre-transition age structure (Wrigley and Schofield type, life expectancy ~30-35) males reaching 18 each year are about 0.9-1.1% of total population. Males only.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: royal caminos reales of Castile and the Spanish Road corridor; mostly unpaved tracks.

majorPorts.note: Seville, Cadiz, Cartagena, Barcelona, Naples, Messina, Palermo, Genoa (allied), Antwerp, Dunkirk, Santander, A Coruna.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Castilian and Basque Atlantic shipping (~175,000-300,000 tons burden c. 1580 in older estimates) plus Italian shipping.

supplyRangeKm.note: van Creveld, Supplying War (isbn:0-521-54657-5) ch. 1: 17th-18th c. armies tied to magazines and bread ovens, operating ~5 marches (~100-150 km) beyond the nearest magazine or navigable river; requisition extends it in rich country. The Spanish Road etapas supplied marching tercios over 1,000 km from Milan to Flanders. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: mules dominated Castilian transport; horses, oxen across 15M people.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row in Iberia and Italy (fortified cities, familiar terrain, popular support); 1.1 or less in the rebel Netherlands.

notes: Snapshot = 1580, the year of the conquest of Portugal (Alba enters Lisbon Aug 1580), before the Portuguese fleet and empire are merged. Population and forces: Castile, Aragon, the Italian possessions (Naples, Sicily, Milan, Sardinia) and the royal-controlled Netherlands; Portugal and the Americas are excluded (Americas as bases only). Personnel convention: salaried troops (Army of Flanders, Italian garrisons, presidios, Alba's army, galley infantry) are active; Italian and Castilian militia are trainedReserves. Army of Flanders strength in 1580 is uncertain because the Spanish tercios had left in 1577-78 and returned in 1582. Parker's paper figures (Military Revolution) are wartime ceilings, not effectives.
